how-much-to-charge-for-an-hvac-maintenan.text:
← HVAC maintenance contract calculator

How much to charge for an HVAC maintenance contract

A maintenance agreement is sold monthly and incurred annually, and that is where the pricing goes wrong. Two tune-ups a year is easy to cost. The covered customer who calls in July is not on the schedule, carries labour and travel, and generates no separate invoice — and an agreement priced without them is priced for a year that will not happen.

Open the free HVAC maintenance contract calculator

Cost the year, then divide by twelve

  1. Scheduled labour: visits per year × hours per visit × loaded hourly rate.
  2. Travel and parts reserve for each of those visits.
  3. Callback visits per year, at their own hours and cost.
  4. Annual overhead the agreement carries.
  5. Divide the annual cost by (1 − target margin) for the yearly price, and by twelve for the monthly quote.

Worked example

Four visits a year at two hours and a $45 loaded rate is $360.00 of scheduled labour, with $20 travel and a $35 parts reserve per visit adding $220.00. One callback of an hour, at $45 of labour and $25 of cost, adds $70.00, and $120.00 of annual overhead brings the yearly cost to $770.00. That is a break-even of $64.17 a month; at a 20% target margin the agreement prices at $962.50 a year, or $80.21 a month. The single callback is worth noticing — it is $70.00 of the $770.00, so an agreement quoted as though callbacks never happen sits about 9% under its own cost before any margin is added at all.

Two things the annual figure hides

Dividing by twelve assumes the customer stays twelve months and that the plan fee is the only money the agreement earns. Neither is usually true, and they pull the price in opposite directions.

The visits are front-loaded. The first tune-up happens the week the agreement is signed, so the contract is underwater from day one and climbs out of it month by month. On the worked example above, break-even arrives in month 5 — a customer who cancels after month 3 has taken two visits ($337.50 of cost) against $240.63 collected, a $96.88 loss on an agreement whose annual margin reads a healthy 20%. That gap is the case for a term commitment, an enrolment fee, or an annual-prepay discount, and no annual figure will ever show it to you.

The plan fee is not the whole return. Members buy repairs and replacements that non-members defer or give to someone else, and that gross profit belongs in the decision even though it does not belong in the plan price. Counting $600 a year of it against the same example drops the floor from $64.17 to $14.17 a month. Both floors matter: the plan-fee floor says whether the visits pay for themselves, and the lower one says whether the member does. Use a figure from your own invoices — a hopeful guess here quietly justifies any price at all.

Common questions

How much should I charge for an HVAC maintenance contract?

Cost a full year of the agreement, then divide by twelve. Add scheduled labour (visits per year × hours per visit × your loaded hourly rate), the travel and parts reserve for each of those visits, the labour and cost of the callbacks the agreement will actually generate, and the annual overhead the contract carries. That annual cost divided by one minus your target margin is the yearly price; a twelfth of it is the monthly figure to quote. Pricing per visit instead of per year is what leaves callbacks uncounted.

Why do HVAC maintenance agreements lose money?

Because the scheduled visits are the predictable part and the callbacks are not, but only the visits get priced. An agreement quoted from two tune-ups a year looks comfortable until the covered customer calls in July; that trip carries labour, travel, and no separate invoice. One callback a year at an hour apiece is a modest assumption, and it still adds real cost to every agreement. Counting an honest callback rate at quoting time is what separates a maintenance base that funds the business from one that consumes the technician hours the business sells.

What is the break-even price on a service agreement?

It is the monthly figure that recovers the annual cost of the agreement with no profit at all — labour, travel, parts reserve, callbacks, and overhead, divided by twelve. It is not the price to sell at; it is the floor to negotiate against. Knowing it lets you discount deliberately, see what each concession costs, and recognise the point at which a competitor's advertised rate cannot be matched without paying for the privilege of holding the account.

How long must a maintenance customer stay before the agreement pays off?

Longer than most contractors assume, because the first tune-up happens at signing. On the worked example — four visits a year at $145 each, priced at $80.21 a month — collected fees do not cover incurred cost until month 5. A cancellation after month 3 leaves two visits delivered, $337.50 of cost against $240.63 collected, and a $96.88 loss on an agreement whose annual margin reads 20%. Annual margin cannot show this, because annual margin assumes a full year of payments against a full year of visits.

Should repair pull-through be counted in the maintenance plan price?

Count it in the decision, not in the plan price. Plan members buy repairs and replacements that non-members defer or take elsewhere, and that gross profit is a real return on the agreement — counting $600 a year of it against the worked example drops the floor from $64.17 to $14.17 a month. Keep both floors visible: the plan-fee floor says whether the visits pay for themselves, and the lower one says whether the member does. Use a figure measured from your own invoices, because a hopeful estimate here can justify any price at all.

Should a maintenance agreement include a parts reserve?

Yes, if the agreement covers filters, belts, contactors, capacitors, or any consumable replaced during a tune-up. A per-visit reserve spreads the predictable small-parts spend across the year, so a visit that happens to need a capacitor does not read as a loss and a visit that needs nothing does not read as unusually profitable. It is a smoothing figure, not an estimate of any one visit, and it belongs in the cost even when the parts are described to the customer as included.

Price the plan, not just the service call.

A free HVAC maintenance contract pricing calculator for independent contractors. After using this, you can now quote a monthly preventive-maintenance agreement that includes technician time, callbacks, parts reserve, and overhead instead of hoping the visits fit inside a flat fee.

How much to charge for an HVAC maintenance contract · This calculator vs. ServiceTitan · This calculator vs. a flat monthly fee

Annual service workload

Risk and margin

Retention and pull-through

Optional. A maintenance plan rarely pays for itself on the plan fee alone — it pays through the repair work a member buys, and it loses money when a member leaves before the visits they have already had are paid for. Leave both blank to price the plan fee on its own.

Common questions

      
What is the difference between the break-even floor and the price at target margin?

      
The break-even floor is annual cost divided by 12 — on the defaults, $770 ÷ 12 = $64.17/month, the price that only covers labor, callbacks, parts, and overhead with zero profit. The target-margin price divides annual cost by (1 − margin) instead — $770 ÷ 0.80 = $962.50/year, or $80.21/month at a 20% margin — so it builds the profit in rather than adding a markup on top.

      
Why does the callback reserve matter if I hope not to need it?

      
Because callbacks happen at a rate you can estimate even when you can't predict which unit fails. On the defaults, 1 expected callback a year at 1 hour and $25 in parts adds $45 labor + $25 = $70 to annual cost — about 9% of the total. Pricing as if callbacks never happen means every real one is unpaid overtime instead of a cost the contract already covers.

      
What does “effective revenue per technician hour” tell me that the monthly price doesn't?

      
It is annual price divided by total technician hours reserved (preventive plus callback) — on the defaults, $962.50 ÷ 9.0 hours = $106.94/hour. That is the number to compare against what the same technician hour earns on a one-off service call; if maintenance-contract hours pay noticeably less than call-out work, the target margin or visit count needs to move before you sign more contracts at this price.

      
What happens if I enter a price a customer is already asking for?

      
The optional field compares that price against your break-even floor and target-margin price, and the page flags it directly when the proposed monthly price falls below break-even — a fast check before agreeing to a number that was set by budget rather than by cost.

      
Does a higher target margin always mean a higher price?

      
Yes, for a fixed annual cost — margin only scales the markup on top of cost, it never reduces it. What changes annual cost itself is the workload: more visits, more technician hours per visit, a higher loaded rate, or more callback reserve. Raise the margin to price in more profit; change the workload assumptions when the cost estimate itself is wrong.

      
How long does a customer have to stay before the plan is profitable?

      
The first tune-up happens at signing, so the agreement is underwater from day one and catches up month by month. On the defaults — 4 visits a year at $145 each, priced at $80.21/month — break-even arrives in month 5. A customer who cancels after month 3 has taken two visits ($337.50 of cost) against $240.63 collected: a $96.88 loss. “Test a cancellation after month” prices that exposure directly. Annual margin cannot show it, because annual margin assumes the customer stays a year.

      
Should I count the repair work a plan member buys?

      
Usually yes, and it often changes the decision. Enter the gross profit — not the revenue — you expect a member to buy in repairs and replacements over a year, and a second floor appears beside the plan-fee floor: on the defaults, $600 of pull-through drops the floor from $64.17 to $14.17/month. Both floors stay on screen because they answer different questions — whether the visits pay for themselves, and whether the member does. If pull-through is a hope rather than a figure you have measured from your own invoices, leave it blank.

      
Is my pricing or customer data uploaded anywhere?

      
No. Everything runs in your browser, and no figures are sent anywhere. “Copy share link” encodes your inputs into this page's own URL hash so a partner or the office can open the same plan; nothing is sent to a server. The only thing recorded is an anonymous local count of which buttons were used — never your rates, customer names, or contract numbers — and it respects Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control.

vs-a-flat-monthly-fee.html.text:
← HVAC Maintenance Contract Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat monthly fee

“$50 a month, every account” is not a price for a maintenance contract — it is a price for one account's visits, technician hours, and callback risk, quietly applied to every account after it.

What a flat monthly fee is

A flat monthly maintenance-plan fee is the fastest way to sell a preventive agreement: pick a round, competitive-sounding number and quote it to every customer. It is easy to advertise, and it is the figure a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set once, off a simple account — one system, a modest visit schedule, little callback history — and then reused for every account afterward, whether the next one has one system or three, four visits a year or eight, and whatever its callback risk turns out to be.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter a plan's preventive visits, technician hours per visit, loaded labor rate, travel, parts reserve, callback risk, annual overhead and target margin. It prices the labor, the reserve, and the overhead as their own lines and returns a break-even floor, a target-margin price, and the exposure of an early cancellation — for this account, not a flat number for every plan under the same name.

What a flat monthly fee doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure whether the account has one system on 4 visits a year or several systems on 8 or more. Prices preventive visits and technician hours at your own rate, so an account with more equipment and more visits costs more — on this account, not a plan-name average.
Has no line for callback risk — a plan with a history of return visits gets the same quote as one that never calls back. Adds a callback reserve as its own line, so repeat-visit risk is already funded rather than eating the plan's margin.
Treats the annual fee as spread evenly across the year, with no line for the fact that the first tune-up happens at signing. Prices an early cancellation directly, showing the cost already incurred against the revenue actually collected by that month.
Bakes an assumed overhead into the flat number rather than your shop's own rate. Applies your own overhead allocation to the account, so the price reflects your burden, not an averaged one.
Gives the salesperson a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the break-even floor and effective revenue per technician hour, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you offer it.

Two accounts, one flat fee

Using this calculator's own defaults, scaled to two account sizes:

A one-system home — 4 preventive visits a year, 2 technician hours each, 1 expected callback — costs $770 a year to service, and this calculator prices it at $80.21 a month ($64.17 break-even floor) at a 20% target margin. A two-system building — 8 visits a year, 2 callbacks, a larger overhead allocation — costs $1,500 a year and this calculator prices it at $156.25 a month ($125.00 break-even floor).

Quote both accounts a flat $50 a month instead and the one-system home brings in $600 a year against its own $770 break-even cost — $170 a year underwater before a dollar of profit. The two-system building brings in the identical $600 a year against a $1,500 break-even cost — a $900-a-year loss. Same flat fee, one account that is merely thin and one that loses money on every visit it gets.

The gap widens further on an early cancellation, because preventive visits are front-loaded: the first tune-up happens at signing, not spread evenly across the year. On the one-system home, a customer who cancels after month 3 has already received two visits worth $337.50 in cost. At the properly priced $80.21 a month, that customer has paid $240.63 by then — a $96.88 loss the contract has already absorbed, which is itself the cost of front-loading. At a flat $50 a month, that same customer has paid only $150 — a $187.50 loss, nearly double, because the lower fee was never checked against the front-loaded cost it has to cover.

Common questions

Why does a flat monthly fee get an HVAC maintenance contract wrong?

Because the cost driver is visit count, technician hours, and callback risk, not "has a maintenance plan." A one-system home on 4 preventive visits a year with a modest callback reserve costs $770 a year to service. A two-system building on 8 visits a year with double the callback reserve costs $1,500 -- almost twice as much -- for the same flat plan-fee marketing copy. A rate that never looks at visit count charges both the same because it was set on neither one.

What does a flat monthly fee usually leave out entirely?

Technician hours per visit, the callback reserve, overhead scaled to the account, and the fact that preventive visits are front-loaded -- the first tune-up happens at signing, before most of a year's fee has been collected. A flat number set once and quoted to every account has no line that moves when the account has more equipment, more callback risk, or cancels early.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own defaults: a one-system home on 4 visits a year costs $770 to service and this calculator prices it at $80.21 a month (20% target margin); a two-system building on 8 visits a year costs $1,500 and prices at $156.25 a month. Quote both a flat $50 a month instead and the one-system account brings in $600 a year against a $770 break-even cost -- $170 a year underwater before any profit -- while the two-system account brings in the same $600 against a $1,500 break-even cost, a $900-a-year loss. Same flat fee, one account that is merely thin and one that loses money on every visit it gets.

Why does an early cancellation hurt more than a flat fee assumes?

Because the first tune-up happens at signing, not spread evenly across the year, so a plan cancelled early has already cost more than a flat monthly fee has collected by then. On the one-system account, a customer who cancels after month 3 has already received two visits worth $337.50 in cost. At the properly priced $80.21 a month, that customer has paid $240.63 by month 3 -- a $96.88 loss the contract has already absorbed. At a flat $50 a month, that same customer has paid only $150 -- a $187.50 loss, nearly double, because the lower fee was never checked against the front-loaded cost it has to cover.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or parts costs?

No. It has no price list and no data on your local labor market or parts supplier pricing. It takes your preventive visits, technician hours, loaded labor rate, callback reserve, parts, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price and an early-cancellation exposure for this account -- the arithmetic a flat monthly fee skips, not a market survey.

← HVAC Maintenance Contract Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based platform for running field service operations, including scheduling, billing and renewing a maintenance agreement once it exists. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should a new preventive-maintenance agreement cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting and a service agreement / membership module that documents a maintenance plan, builds out its recurring visits for the contract term, and automates billing and renewal reminders. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole business, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity, category and publicly described service-agreement features are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that service-agreement software describe managing, scheduling and billing a plan once its terms and price already exist; none describe a step that works out what a new agreement should cost from technician time, callback risk, parts reserve and target margin before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, send renewal reminders, or invoice a customer. It takes one maintenance plan's preventive visits, technician hours per visit, loaded labor rate, travel, parts reserve, callback risk, annual overhead and target margin, and turns that into a break-even monthly floor, a target-margin monthly and annual price, technician hours reserved, and effective revenue per technician hour — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to schedule technicians, send renewal reminders, and invoice customers for maintenance agreements across my whole business.ServiceTitan, or a comparable field service platform — running that ongoing operation is not something this calculator does.

A customer's budget is below what I'd normally quote. Does it still clear my break-even floor?This calculator's proposed-price check — it flags a price below break-even before you agree to it.
I already have agreements priced and need to track, bill and renew them across many customers, over time.ServiceTitan — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a maintenance-contract price actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. ServiceTitan's tools are used through an account.

Most contractors running maintenance agreements get different value from each: ServiceTitan (or a comparable field service platform) for scheduling, billing and renewing agreements across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what a new agreement should cost before it is offered. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed contract, an invoice, or a claim about what a customer owes.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and most HVAC contractors who run maintenance agreements at any scale end up touching both. ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan and headquartered in Glendale, California, used by HVAC, plumbing, electrical and other trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing and reporting across a business. Its service agreement and membership software documents, schedules and bills a maintenance plan on an ongoing basis once the plan's terms and price already exist — automating renewal reminders and recurring visit scheduling. It is an account-based platform you sign up for and use continuously. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a plan's preventive visits, technician hours, loaded labor rate, callback reserve, parts, travel, overhead and target margin, and turns that into a break-even floor, a target-margin price and an effective revenue per technician hour, before you have quoted anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A contractor who already has a priced agreement and needs to schedule, bill and renew it across many customers is better served by ServiceTitan or a comparable field service platform; a contractor who needs an instant, private answer to what a new agreement should cost before it is offered is in the right place here.
